To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

storm discharges of PON, POP, and PNH 4 increased up to 2 orders of magnitude in storm events, while concentrations of DON, DPi, and DOP did not increase much, and that the concentrations of PON and POP increased significantly with peak discharge among storms.

the concentrations of dissolved and particulate organic N and P forms increased up to 10-fold in storm events, while concentrations of nitrate, dissolved and particulate ammonnium, and inorganic P forms did not change verymuch.

storm discharges of N and P were dominated by organic forms, especially particulate forms, that the highest N and P discharges were from the most intensely cultivated watershed, and that the concentrations of N and P increased with storm discharge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of land use on nutrient transport from watersheds during storms.
nutrient export from watersheds in relation to storm events.
the fate of nitrogen and phosphorus in the Rhode River watershed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

storm discharges of PON, POP, and PNH _{4} from the Rhode River watershed are significantly correlated with peak water discharge, but that storm discharges from other watersheds may be more or less correlated with peak discharge depending on the land use and the storm event.

the highest concentrations of N and P were discharged in the largest storms from watersheds with the most croplan, while the highest concentrations of P were discharged from the most grazed watershed.

the concentrations of PON, POP, DNH4 and PNH.4 increased significantly with increasing peak water discharge, but the concentrations of DON, DOP, DPi, and nitrate did NOT increase with increasing peak water discharges.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PON and POP are the dominant N and P forms in storm discharges, and that the ratios of TN to TP and TIN to TIP decline with increasing water discharge.

PON and POP are the dominant forms of nitrogen and phosphorus in storm discharges and that their concentrations increase significantly with peak discharge, while concentrations for DON, DOP, DPi, nitrate, and DNH4 are not related to peak discharge.
the dominant forms of nitrogen in storm discharges were PON, DOP, and nitrate, and the dominant forms of phosphorus were POP and PPi.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the forms of nitrogen and phosphorus that are most important for water quality in streams are those that are most easily mobilized from soils and that these forms change in response to changes in land use.
PON and POP dominate storm discharges from these watersheds, but that the concentrations of these forms vary greatly with season, land use, and storm intensity.
the concentrations of particulate N and P increased dramatically during storms, and these particulates may contribute substantially to N and P loads in estuaries.
